parts.note: Tobias Smollett wrote a novel about Ferdinand, Count of this name, and the name is also the six-foot unit by which sea depths were sounded

explanation.walkthrough: Smollett's 1753 novel is 'The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom'; to sound the sea is to measure its depth, which is done in six-foot units, so the Count's surname is the measure that was sounded.
explanation.definitionFit: The Count is Smollett's title character, and the same word names the nautical depth unit and the verb meaning to sound.

clue.text: As a game with no double services?

definitions.text: As a game with no double services?

parts.words: As a game with no double services?
parts.note: in tennis two bad serves in a row lose the point, and a game free of those has no such errors

explanation.walkthrough: In tennis a double fault is two failed serves in a row; a game with none is free of faults, the adjective meaning perfect.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfect play has no errors, which in tennis means no double faults.

clue.text: Renoir half in the air, portraying a French soldier

indicators.note: in tells you one piece goes inside another

parts.note: an air is a tune

indicators.note: half takes the first half of the painter's name

explanation.surface: A painter of Renoir's style depicts a French military figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Renoir' tempts you toward painters, but only the first half of his name is used. Turenne was a great 17th-century marshal of France.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri de la Tour d'Auvergne, Vicomte de Turenne, was a celebrated marshal of France.

definitions.meaning: Sir William Quiller ..., a Scottish portrait and genre painter
a boy born of fruit trees would be the son of a fruit garden

explanation.walkthrough: Read the name as two words: the child of a garden of fruit trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir William Quiller Orchardson was a Victorian Scottish artist, and his surname splits into a fruit-tree garden plus its boy.

definitions.meaning: a genus of shrubs and small trees, Euonymus, whose hard wood was used for spinning pins
rods on a spinning wheel that revolve to wind thread on

explanation.walkthrough: 'wind' rhymes with 'kind' here, as in winding yarn, not the breeze that trees bend in.
explanation.definitionFit: The Euonymus shrub is called by this name, and the same word names the rotating rods on which yarn is wound.

clue.text: Begetters of a gap in one's reading

indicators.note: in tells you one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a page is what one reads
a rent is a tear, a gap

explanation.surface: Ancestors explain a missing leaf in a family book.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is collective: one's mother and father as a body, which is why the plural 'Begetters' fits a singular noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means lineage, the parents collectively, those who begot one.

parts.note: add the word gay to this body part and you get a small bunch of flowers

explanation.walkthrough: A nosegay is a posy; the body part is the word that, with 'gay', makes the flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: The organ of smell joins 'gay' to make a nosegay, a small bouquet of blossoms.

parts.note: Robin Goodfellow, Puck, is called 'thou lob of spirits' in A Midsummer Night's Dream
Charles Lamb wrote his essays as Elia

explanation.surface: Two literary figures, a sprite and an essayist, meet among the flowerbeds.
explanation.walkthrough: Robin Goodfellow (Puck) is addressed as 'lob of spirits' by a fairy in Shakespeare; Charles Lamb signed his essays 'Elia'. The answer is a blue bedding plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A low-growing blue-flowered bedding plant, so something found growing in the garden.

parts.note: the rose oil of 9 is noticed by the organ of 6 through its smell

explanation.walkthrough: 9 is attar (otto) of roses and 6 the nose; the oil is detected through its smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A perfume is perceived by smell, the quality the nose picks up from rose oil.

parts.note: a man's name that is also attar, an essential oil of roses used in perfume

explanation.walkthrough: Otto is a man's name and also attar, the essential oil of roses; 'Essentially' points to an essence, not to 'basically'.
explanation.definitionFit: Attar of roses, an essence used in scent, shares its spelling with a man's first name.

clue.text: The curt made urbane by the Dutch

definitions.text: The curt made urbane by the Dutch

indicators.note: turning the letters into a city (made urban) and so into a new arrangement signals the reshuffle

explanation.surface: Dutch manners polish a brusque visitor into a smooth gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made urbane' looks like a remark on manners; it signals that the letters of THE CURT are rebuilt, and the result is a Dutch city, an urban place.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in the central Netherlands, so a place the Dutch made into a town.

parts.note: Minnehaha in Longfellow's Hiawatha means Laughing Water, so water that laughs is given to mirth

explanation.walkthrough: Minnehaha, the heroine of Longfellow's 'Song of Hiawatha', has a name meaning 'Laughing Water'; the drink is the water, and the laughing gives the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means laughing or given to laughter, which describes the water of Minnehaha's name.

clue.text: The French put so much on a horse as equivalent

parts.note: the French word for 'so much' is tant, as the clue's 'The French' signals
a mount is a horse for riding

explanation.surface: A Frenchman stakes an equal sum on a horse at the races.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French' tells you to give 'so much' in French, TANT; that is put on A MOUNT, a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Something amounting to the same value as another is equal or equivalent to it.

clue.text: The way the small change goes!

definitions.text: The way the small change goes!

parts.words: The way the small change goes!
parts.note: coins disappear into the narrow opening of a vending or ... machine

explanation.walkthrough: 'small change' reads as minor alterations, but it is the coins, and the way they go is through the narrow opening of a machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow opening into which coins are dropped is the passage the loose change goes through.

parts.note: Wodehouse wrote a novel about a Jim named after a London street, and the street was named after an old stiff collar

explanation.walkthrough: P. G. Wodehouse wrote 'Piccadilly Jim'; the London street took its name from the piccadill, a stiff lace collar, so the item would be worn by Jim.
explanation.definitionFit: The piccadill was a 17th-century ruffed collar, a garment, and Wodehouse's hero bears the street name derived from it.

clue.text: Corrected backward me and had done

indicators.note: backward tells you to write the word me from right to left

parts.note: had done means finished, ended

explanation.surface: Someone owns up to amending their work in a muddled order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' turns ME into EM, and 'had done' gives ENDED.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct its errors, so the past tense means put right.

clue.text: Hereditary determinants of the brown cow south of Kent

parts.note: a dun cow is a greyish-brown one
genes determine inherited traits

explanation.surface: Biology lesson on what makes a brown cow brown, set in southern Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'south' looks like part of the place description, but it supplies S. Dungeness is a shingle headland on the Kent coast in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: A shingle headland on the Kent coast, home to a lighthouse and power station, so a place belonging to the county.

parts.note: the creatures that went into Noah's ark two by two, like a crocodile of schoolchildren walking in pairs

explanation.walkthrough: A crocodile in Britain is a line of schoolchildren walking in pairs; the beasts of the Flood boarded the ark two by two, the first such line of refugees.
explanation.definitionFit: Beasts entering the ark in pairs formed the first refugee column, a crocodile walking two abreast.

parts.note: rates read as rates of travel, and the overseers are police who watch them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rates' suggests local property taxes in Britain; here it is how fast drivers go, watched by traffic police.
explanation.definitionFit: Traffic police monitor motorists' velocity, so they oversee rates of travel.

parts.note: sand is what a beach is made of
something private is one's own

explanation.surface: An exclusive stretch of shore on a holiday island.
explanation.walkthrough: I.O.W. is the Isle of Wight, off England's south coast; the answer is a resort town there, and also a racecourse in Surrey.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaside town on the Isle of Wight, so a place found in I.O.W.

parts.note: a battle near Durham in 1346 is named after a man's cross

explanation.walkthrough: The Battle of Neville's Cross (1346), near Durham in northern England, is named after a stone cross; the man's name is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The battle site near Durham is called after this man's cross, so his name plus 'cross' gives the battle.

parts.note: a piece of territory surrounded on all sides by a foreign state

explanation.definitionFit: Such a district lies entirely within another country's borders, so it is the thing encircled.

clue.text: A quintet of relatives hops it

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five, a quintet
aunts are relatives

explanation.surface: A family of five aunts all leave together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Avaunt!' is an old word for 'Begone!', so the verb is to clear off; 'hops it' is British slang for leaving quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic verb of departure, so clears off or leaves quickly.

parts.note: flag read as a flagstone; to lay flagstones down is to surface a path

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag down' looks like stopping a taxi; a flag is also a paving stone, and laying it down surfaces a path.
explanation.definitionFit: To surface a road or path with flat stones is the act of laying flagstones down.

parts.note: to pip is to fail or blackball, as in an examination

explanation.surface: Someone flunks a test just for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lark' looks like a prank; it is the bird, as the pipit is a lark-like songbird (titlark).
explanation.definitionFit: The pipit is a small brown songbird resembling a lark, once called a titlark.

definitions.meaning: a polite person yawns with a hand covering the mouth

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is read as two words: a well-mannered yawn is done behind a hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in arrears means running late, and courtesy puts a palm before a yawning mouth.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Part of foot or chin (4)': INCH is part of a foot, and its letters rearrange CHIN, but no word signals the anagram except 'Part', which is already the definition, so one word does two jobs.

clue.text: Keep on and on with pluck

definitions.meaning: to go on about something tediously
a stringed instrument played by plucking

explanation.walkthrough: 'pluck' reads as courage; it is plucking strings.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell on a subject tiresomely is to harp on, and the large stringed instrument is played by plucking.

parts.note: a pill is a dose of a drug, dope
an era is an age

explanation.surface: A druggy period of history ends in getting the sack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sack' is the verb to plunder, not dismissal.
explanation.definitionFit: To sack a town is to plunder it, which is what looting troops do.

clue.text: Battleground where the colonel's lost fifty and is in trouble

indicators.note: being in trouble suggests disorder, so the remaining letters are rearranged
lost tells you a piece goes missing from the colonel's letters

parts.note: the possessive s is kept as a letter
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: An officer loses half his hundred men and finds himself in difficulty on the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost' removes one L (fifty) from COLONELS to leave COLONES, which 'in trouble' rearranges. Colenso, in Natal, was a Boer War battle of 1899 where the British were beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: Colenso in South Africa was the site of a Boer War battle, so a battle site.

clue.text: Take very French leave — and get prosecuted?

definitions.text: Take very French leave — and get prosecuted?

parts.note: the French word for very is tres
a pass is permission to be absent, leave

explanation.surface: Someone sneaks off without permission and ends up in court.
explanation.walkthrough: TRES is French for 'very' and a PASS is leave; taking French leave means going without permission, and notices warn that those who go uninvited will be prosecuted.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter land without permission is to take a liberty, and signs warn such intruders will be prosecuted.

indicators.note: in tells you one word sits inside another

parts.note: eyes are the organs of vision

explanation.surface: Fledgling birds of prey seen in a sharp-eyed sense.
explanation.walkthrough: An eyas is a falconer's word for a nestling hawk; 'vision' stands for the organs that see, not for sight itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A falconer's term for a nestling hawk taken for training, so young birds of prey.
